title: [Must Read] System Design Interview Preparation Guide
page_content:
### System Design Interview Preparation Guide  

I spent a couple of months preparing for system design interviews, and let me tell you—it’s a journey. Over time, I went through *a ton* of resources but eventually narrowed it down to a few game-changers that made all the difference. Thanks to these, I ended up landing offers from multiple big tech companies.  

The LeetCode community has been super helpful throughout my prep, so I wanted to give back with this post. If you’re gearing up for system design interviews, here’s a list of awesome resources and tips that’ll help you crush it.  

---

#### 1. **The Basics**  
##### 1a. *System Design Primer by Donne Martin*  
- Link: [System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)  
- Start here. Don’t even bother looking anywhere else. Just open this link and go through *every single topic* mentioned.  
- The fundamentals are what set you apart in interviews. Knowing the "what" and "why" behind concepts will make you a stronger candidate.  
- This guide is super detailed, and the step-by-step explanations are gold. It’s all about building a rock-solid foundation.  
- Pro tip: Interviewers love to dive into details about your solutions. So, trust me—get those foundational concepts crystal clear before tackling problems.  

##### 1b. *Designing Data-Intensive Applications (DDIA)*  
- This book by Martin Kleppmann is *next level*. It’s perfect for understanding data systems, distributed systems, and database design.  
- If you can read it cover to cover, you’re basically on your way to becoming a system design expert. Seriously, every page is a gem.  
- If you’re short on time, skim it. But if you can, make it a habit to read it a little every day—it’s totally worth it.  

---

#### 2. **Amazing Videos**  
- [System Design Interview - YouTube Channel](https://www.youtube.com/@SystemDesignInterview)  
  - Run by Mikhail, this channel is just *chef’s kiss*. He’s also the instructor for LeetCode’s premium system design course.  
  - There aren’t many videos, but each one is packed with knowledge bombs. Watch them carefully and absorb every single solution he explains.  
  - Heads up: A 30-minute video might take hours to fully digest because you’ll want to pause, research, and explore related topics. Totally worth it, though.  

---

#### 3. **Alex Xu: The OG**  
- Once you’ve got your basics down, grab both versions of Alex Xu’s system design books.  
- The second book is especially detailed and a must-read.  
- Here’s the hack: If the book mentions, say, distributed transactions using 2PC, go the extra mile and dive deep into 2PC. Expand your understanding beyond the pages.  

---

#### 4. **Hello Interview Channel: Structuring Your Approach**  
- [Hello Interview - YouTube Channel](https://www.youtube.com/@hello_interview)  
  - This channel is all about how to structure your approach during system design interviews.  
  - Once your basics are solid, these videos will help you level up your presentation, communication, and visual representation skills.  
  - If you want to sound like a senior engineer during interviews, watch these.  

---

#### 5. **Practice, Practice, and Practice**  
- Mock interviews are your best friend. Practice with friends, coworkers, or even your parents (yes, really). The more you practice presenting your ideas, the better.  
- Platforms like Exponent offer free mock interviews—take advantage of them.  
- For diagrams, I swear by Excalidraw. It’s hands down the best tool for this.  

---

#### 6. **The Interview**
- Most of the interviews will be of 1-hour duration. 
- Time breakdown:
	- Introduction: 5-10mins ( try to be super duper fast with the introduction so that you can save those precious minutes for later, trust me an interview ends before you could realize whats going on!!)
	- Problem statement: 5mins ( Ask clarifying questions and make sure you have an agreement with the interview on what are you going to design. Failing to have this agreement will lead to mis-communications and multiple iterations later on)
	- Time window for you to ask questions to the interviewer at the end: 5min.

- If you see you will only have 35min-40min to do the actual desing. So make sure you manager your time well. Whatever be your style of interviews, make sure you have an AGREEMENT with the interviewer.
- Lets say you feel you dont need back of the envelope estimation right now and defer it for later, communicate to the interviewer that you will take it up later when needed and doing that calculation might not be useful.
- Treat your interviews as your team mate and make sure you take his/her thoughts and go ahead before moving forward.
- You have 30mins to show your NINJA-level system design skills that you have learnt over the past few months of hardwork, so make sure you speak up and keep communicating a lot. So keep the COMMUNICATION going. 
- Drive the interview, be on the PILOT seat. Interviews like it when you drive the interview and they just help you with minor inputs. Incase you feel you are expert in an area, drive the interview towards that direction
- Be prepared to get grilled or interviewers who make you uneasy or put you in a tough spot. Does not matter how much you getting grilled, keep smiling and moving forward. Dont get nervous and give it all. I have done the mistake and paid the price. So, be calm, composed and continue the momentum.
- So summarizing these are the important things in the interview:
	- Be Confident
	- Make an agreement with the interviewer.
	- Clarify
	- Communicate, Communicate and Communicate
	- Close and conclude the design with a brief walk through.
	- Complete the interview, and get the offer you have been working hard for.


In case you wanna stay connected, please drop your linkedIn profile, I will send you a connection request. 

Follow these resources and tips, and you’ll be ready to crush your system design interviews. You’ve got this!

title: Sprinklr | Product Intern'25 | Interview Experience
page_content:
***Company: Sprinklr
Job Profile: Product Intern (2 Months)
Compensation: 1.5L pm
College: Tier 1.5
Opportunity: On-campus, open for all***

# OA

There were two questions one was easy-medium binary search question and the other was a hard graph question. I was able to solve both of them and a total of 30 students were shortlisted from our campus.

# Round 1

The round started with a basic introduction, I had some work experience so the interviewer discussed that with me. A few questions were - 

```
1. How do you manage API Calls?
2. Is http.post and http.get scalable?
```

Then we moved to a DSA question, the interview was held on an online notepad with screen sharing enabled.

The question was an easy sliding window based question, there were a couple of edge cases in the question but I managed to identify them and performed a dry run to the interviewer. The interviewer was satisfied with my approach and moved on to a puzzle question.

**Q -** There are 3 light bulbs (R,G,B) with 3 switches respectively. Let 000 signify all are off and 111 signify all are on. If more than one bulb are turned on you will see a mixture of those colors. You have to go from 000 to 111 covering all possible colors in the shortest number of moves such that in one move you can toggle only one bulb.

This clearly reminded me of the gray code sequence and I was instantly able to answer it and the interviewer was impressed by it. 

I was selected for the next round which was in about 1.5 hrs.

# Round 2

This round started initially with discussion about my projects. I explained the tech stack, project structure, the goal of the project, etc. and in the meantime the interviewer had opened the same project on Github and asked me a couple of questions over my react and flutter projects - 
```
1. What does package.json / pubspec.yaml file store.
2. What does package-lock.json / pubspec.lock file store.
3. What is the difference between the two.
4. What is the difference between dependencies and dev-dependencies.
5. How do you send real time notifications if the app is currently in dead state.
```

I was only able to answer a couple of them and the interviewer was already disappointed. He then moved on to a DSA question .

Q - A database contains the list of all batters and their respective runs scored by them. We have to define a data structure so as to minimize the time complexity of the following operations - 

```
1. Add a batter to the db
2. Remove a batter from the db
3. getRunsScored(String batter)
4. kthHighestRunScorer(int k)
```

I took around 10 mins but was able to devise a data structure, the interviewer didn’t really respond to my answer and straightaway moved to the next question. The final question was a puzzle question. 

Q - Alice and Bob are playing a game where during their turn a player selects any number between 1 to 10 ( both inclusive) and add it to the currentSum. Whenever the currentSum reaches 100 the player with the present turn wins. Alice always starts first, derive a strategy for alice so that she never loses. 

I was able to deduce that alice need to reach 89 in order to win, after that i started thinking about multiples and factors and hence couldn’t find the correct approach. 

The answer was to recursively solve for alice. 

100 —> 89 —> 78 …. —> 12 —> 1. 

Felt really bad that i couldn’t solve the puzzle as it was very easy.

The interview ended here and I was informed by the Placement team that I was rejected.

**My Google SWE L4 Interview Experience**

I recently had the opportunity to interview for the Software Engineer L4 role at Google. As of now, the final verdict is pending, but I wanted to share my experience to help others prepare for a similar journey.
YoE: 4.5

**Phone Screen**

The initial phone screen included a technical question combining Tree DFS and Binary Search. I received **positive** feedback for this round, which boosted my confidence for the subsequent steps. Following this, I was informed that my onsite interviews were scheduled for a month later, giving me ample time to prepare.

**Onsite Interviews**

***1st Technical Round:***
The problem was the classic Knight Tour Problem on an infinite grid. Although I managed to propose a solution, the feedback was rated as **average**. It was a challenging start to the onsite rounds.

***2nd Technical Round:***
This round took me by surprise. Instead of a DSA-focused problem, it turned out to be a class design question. I was asked to design a Task Scheduler. Thankfully, system design is one of my strong suits. I confidently tackled the problem, and the feedback was **highly positive**. A definite highlight of the process!

***3rd Technical Round:***
The focus shifted back to trees. I was given a Tree-Based Subtree Deletion problem, followed by a detailed discussion on follow-up scenarios. My solution and approach received **positive** feedback, keeping my spirits high.

***G&L Round:***
The final round was the Googliness and Leadership (G&L) interview. While I felt the conversation went well, I was later informed that the feedback for this round was **negative**. This was disheartening, especially since I had been performing well up to this point.

**Current Status**

After learning about the feedback from the G&L round, I reached out to my recruiter to request another opportunity for this round. I am currently waiting to hear back regarding the next steps.

**Reflections**

* Preparation is key, but adaptability is just as important. The unexpected class design round was a curveball, but my prior experience worked in my favor.
* Interviews at Google can be as much about soft skills and alignment with company values as they are about technical expertise.
* Communication with the recruiter is crucial if you feel you have room for improvement or deserve another shot.

I hope this provides insights into the Google SWE L4 interview process. If you’re preparing for similar interviews, focus on both technical and behavioral aspects, and don’t hesitate to advocate for yourself if needed.

Problem 1: A tree problem requiring level order traversal and indegree calculations. I proposed multiple approaches, including reversing the level order traversal. After explaining why the final approach was optimal, I implemented the solution. This took about 40 minutes.

title: Software Engineer || PR1 || Cimpress
page_content:
My Interview Experience at Cimpress.

**Background:**

*   College: NIT-B
*   Current Company/Role: Infosys/SP L1
*   Years of Experience: 3.1 (2.3 at Infosys) got 3% hike in 2023 Dec, no appraisal/promitions till now.
*   On notice period without any offer.
*   Current CTC: 10 LPA (including 1.5 LPA variable pay)
*   Expected CTC: 15 LPA

I applied for a role at Cimpress and initially requested 15 LPA. The recruiter stated they could offer a 30-35% hike on my current CTC or I could proceed with a DSA round. I opted for the DSA round.

**Round 1: DSA (Two Interviewers)**

*   **Problem 1:** Add two numbers represented as linked lists. I solved this quickly.
*   **Problem 2:** Given an array of 0s and 1s, find the minimum number of iterations to convert all 0s to 1s. A 0 can be replaced with a 1 in an iteration if it has a 1 on either adjacent side (without considering changes in the current iteration). I discussed a solution covering all edge cases, which the interviewers were satisfied with.
*   The interviewers also asked questions about my resume and current projects.

Within 10 minutes, the HR contacted me with positive feedback and scheduled a design round for four days later. Surprisingly, she explicitly mentioned the design question would be a Low-Level Design (LLD) of a shopping cart. I found this unusual but prepared for various LLD problems nonetheless.

**Round 2: Design (Two Interviewers)**

*   The interviewers presented a scenario similar to OYO.
*   **High-Level Design (HLD):** I was asked to provide an HLD & LLD for the application, including the screens, their interactions with the backend, and the backend's HLD.
    *   While drawing the high-level components, the interviewers interrupted and asked me to focus on entities instead.
    *   I jumpeed on LLD then.
    *   I began defining attributes for each class, planning to refine them as I progressed.
    *   I generalized "User" into "Customer" and "Receptionist" classes. The interviewers questioned this, suggesting a single "User" class with a "userType" attribute. We discussed the trade-offs of both approaches.
    *   They then shifted the focus to the required database tables.
    *   Given a scenario, they asked about the fields needed to store a "Hotel," including "location." They then asked about the appropriate database type for storing location data. I explained that while longitude and latitude could be stored in a NoSQL database for better location-based queries, I would consider a simpler approach for the interview context.
    *   This led to a discussion about database technologies, focusing on read/write operations, latency, the CAP theorem, and data storage strategies like columnar storage for ETL. This discussion consumed a significant amount of time.
    *   They then asked me to write a function to list available hotels in a specific location.
    *   Due to time constraints, they presented another scenario: given existing bookings for a single room, determine if a new booking is possible based on dates. I provided a solution involving sorting check-in dates and checking for overlaps.
    *   At the end, I asked for feedback. The interviewers stated that HR would share it.

I felt the design round was rushed and didn't go as well as I had hoped. I felt I was interrupted and redirected frequently, preventing me from fully articulating my design.

I attempted to contact HR for feedback regarding the explicit mention of the shopping cart LLD, but received no response. I felt this practice was unprofessional.

An hour later, I received a rejection email without any specific feedback from the interviewers. I emailed HR requesting feedback but received no reply.

**Key Learnings for Design Rounds:**

*   Time management is crucial.
*   Adopting a top-down approach and maintaining a consistent flow, even when interrupted, is important.
*   It's questionable whether 1.5 hours is sufficient to thoroughly discuss HLD, LLD, and all screens for a complex application like OYO, especially given the interview was scheduled for only 1 hour.
*   Consistent practice of various design problems, from high-level to detailed implementation and technology choices, is essential.

This revised version is more concise, professional, and focuses on the facts of the interview experience. It removes the emotional commentary while still highlighting the key issues and learnings.

Keep striving and anticipate the best!

title: [Part-II] Journey from 4L to 90L -  Life is marathon not sprint.
page_content:
**[Part-I]** : https://leetcode.com/discuss/interview-experience/1464918/Journey-from-4L-to-40L-Life-is-marathon-not-sprint.

First, I would like to congratulate all the folks (90+ in count) who, despite starting as below average in their careers (with WITCH or similar organizations), got inspired by the above post, took action, and secured a good offer. This post is targeted at experienced professionals who are willing to switch.

I am continuing this as many of you requested for an update on my journey. It has been 3+ years since Part 1, and here I am with the second edition, now with a total of 6 years and a few months of experience.

**Sept 2021:** Joined a new organization with a 40L salary. It was relatively a startup, so I had to grind for long hours. Since my past experience wasn’t very strong, I used to dedicate 12+ hours to work almost daily. It was remote due to COVID, so I could invest significant time in my work.

**Dec 2021:** Tried for Google and Microsoft. I cleared Microsoft technical rounds, but the manager declined due to my frequent switches. Google feedback was mixed: 2 strong hire, 1 lean hire, and 1 no-hire. I wasn’t able to practice alongside work and got bored of DSA that year.

**June 2022:** Received a 10% increment, bringing my current salary to around 44L. I started considering a switch as remote work was about to end, and I was feeling homesick. I was tired of the poor work-life balance (WLB). Over the next 4-5 months, I interviewed at many places and received offers from Adobe, PhonePe, Deliveroo, Ethos, LendingKart, and others. I declined Adobe (though it offered good money) as they wanted me to work on a desktop app in C++.

**Dec 2022:** Took a 15-day break and joined a new remote job with 52L in the new year. It was another startup but much better than the last one. Pay wasn’t the main factor; remote work was. To be honest, I was scared of the culture.

I continued working there for 2 years and got a promotion, though it didn’t come with a significant hike (only 10%). The work was awesome—I delivered ~50 features, improved on-call processes, and learned many great things. This was the first time I experienced how you can be efficient even without daily standup meetings. This restored my faith that corporate people can be technically sound and humble at the same time.

**Nov 2024:** Finally left the remote job and moved to a hybrid role with a bigger brand and a tempting & whopping offer of 88-90L. I received an offer from Blinkit for 70-75L but declined it due to its horrible culture and 5-day office policy. Switching out of remote work was a tough choice but necessary as I was falling behind in terms of learning and networking.

[FAQ]:

**1. Did I face challenges switching so many times in my short career?**
Yes, of course. I faced a lot of rejections in screening rounds because of my unstable profile, which gets highlighted at the first glance. I even faced rejection at Microsoft for the same reason, with the manager stating it directly.

**2. How did I get so many interview calls? Where did I apply?**
I did everything to get interview calls: Naukri, Instahyre, LinkedIn DMs, referrals, LinkedIn jobs. It was a mix of all these efforts. I don’t have any magic portals. The remote job was also a coincidence. Influencer posts claiming "Top 10 sites for remote jobs" were of no use to me—don’t fall for that trap.

**3. How did I learn DSA?**
The most frequent question I get is how I learned DSA: I learned during COVID, as shared in my last post. Since 2021, I haven’t practiced much. Posting without anonymity so you can see how little I’ve practiced in the last 4 years. Contests helped me retain my logical thinking for new problems in interviews. My practice tapered off in 2021 and decreased further in 2022-23-24. I plan to improve in 2025.

**4. Resources for System Design?**
I believe everyone knows the resources—ask ChatGPT, and it’ll tell you the same. There are free and paid resources; choose one and stick with it. Don’t switch midway.
For me, as I mentioned in my last post, I prefer books for better concentration. I learned concepts through books (still a work in progress). I fell in love with technical books. I learned system design mostly on the job through code reviews and feedback on architectures I designed.

**5. How did I find time to prepare?**
I used to code early in the morning. That’s why my username reflects this habit—it’s tough for me to work after office hours, as my mind doesn’t function well then. For the 2024 switch, I casually interviewed without specific preparation.

**6. Did I take any academy or paid training?**
Never. I’m not a fan of paid training. You can use them for discipline, but free resources are also sufficient.

**7. Do I mentor people or give paid training to engineers?**
No, I’ve never done personal paid training. I tried a few academies but didn’t like their curriculums (not student-friendly), so I didn’t continue. I’ve helped a few individuals who were proactive but stuck, usually over weekends to solve their coding issues.

**8. Can I reveal my personal info, LinkedIn, or company names?**
No, sorry. I’m uncomfortable sharing these details. Please don’t ask. Maintaining anonymity is tough for me, especially when not posting anonymously. Feel free to ask questions; I’ll answer them.

**9. Is it recommended to switch jobs this frequently?**
No, never. Frequent switches are not good for your profile, it portrays you as unstable. Unfortunately, your next salary is decided by your previous salary. I started with such a low salary that switching was the only way to step-up. Had I started with 6-9L, I would not have switched so often. 

**10. My tech stack and years of experience?**
I have 6.5 years of experience. My tech stack has been primarily Java microservices backend with Kafka, REST, and gRPC. I’m open to other backend systems as well (tech-agnostic).

**11. What’s the significance of this post?**
Some might call this show-off, but I’m not an influencer or trying to sell courses. I’m sharing this because I’m one of you, believing 30-40L is the end goal. My earning target in college was 30-35L, but life took threw in some surprises. The harder you work, the luckier you get!

**12. When should you look at the solution to a coding problem?**
There are two phases for every topic: learning and practice. During the learning phase, feel free to look at solutions and understand them (try brute force if you can). In the practice phase, avoid looking at solutions immediately. If you have a clue, try coding or dry running your solution. Don’t jump to solutions directly.

Clearing misconceptions from my DMs:

*  *This journey was smooth and easy.* **No, it was tough** Even today, if I apply to 40-50 companies on LinkedIn/Naukri, I get one recruiter call, which often ends with ghosting. It’s a devastating feeling. Rejections from big companies were significant disappointments.
*  *You must be living a great life.* Not really. My in-hand salary is much less after taxes and other deductions. I gained weight, lost touch with friends, and barely traveled.
* Hopefully, in 2025, I’ll get back in shape and find someone to move to the next phase of life with Bhagwan ji’s blessings.
* There are folks earning far better than me, with deeper knowledge. I’m still a beginner, not an expert.
* I’m not familiar with front-end, data science, or AI roles, so I can’t share opinions on them. My experience is limited to QA manual, support, and backend dev positions.

***It’s never too late to hit a few sixes in life!***

Discipline beats motivation. If you’re motivated, start solving one question daily in 2025, and share your offers with me—I love seeing dreams fulfilled. 
Wish you all a very happy 2025 !!

title: Twilio Interview: My Experience and Preparation Tips (Dec'24)
page_content:
I recently interviewed at Twilio—an opportunity that thrilled me. The interview process included four consecutive 45-minute interviews, which all shortlisted candidates had to complete.

Education: M. Tech. from Tier 1 college (On campus opportinuty)
Years of Experience: Fresher

1. Coding round I (55 mins)
2. Coding round II (50 mins)
3. System design round (1 hour)
4. Managerial Round (55 mins)

**For both coding rounds**, the interviewer shared a HackerRank link containing medium-difficulty LeetCode problems. These weren't standard questions you'd typically find in coding sheets. 

The expectations for each coding round are clear—passing all test cases generally indicates a successful interview. My experience was quite positive, as the interviewers were friendly and willing to provide hints when needed. For instance, in the second round, when I couldn't pass all the test cases on my first attempt, the interviewer discussed my approach and offered helpful guidance.

How to Prepare: Solving medium to hard LeetCode questions across all DSA topics will help you clear such interviews. Be vocal during the process and be ready to explain the reasoning behind each line of code you write. 

The **system design round** varies across companies and interviewers. Some interviews focus on low-level design of specific software components, such as a ticket booking module in BookMyShow. In my interview, they provided a single table schema and asked me to design a database from it. While I could create multiple tables from the initial schema, I needed to clearly explain my thought process and reasoning behind each design decision. (Just design not SQL code)

They evaluated my understanding of database concepts, including normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF), table dependencies, and primary keys. The focus was on demonstrating how data can be stored efficiently to ensure better manageability. 

How to prepare: Study core computer science fundamentals like databases, concurrency, caching, and memory management. Then focus on learning low-level design patterns. 

The **managerial round** tests your experience and behavioral consistency across different situations. In my interview, they asked questions about my previous internship experiences and how I handled various scenarios. Some example questions included: "How would you help a teammate who struggles to express their work clearly?" and "Have you ever had a conflict with your team lead during your previous internship, and how did you resolve it?"

How to prepare: Think carefully before speaking to avoid contradicting yourself later. It's perfectly fine to take a few minutes to gather your thoughts before answering questions during the interview. Being thoughtful and consistent is more important than giving quick responses.

title: Disappointing Interview Experience with Microsoft
page_content:
Hi All, I wanted to share my experience from a recent interview I had with Microsoft for the SSE role. Unfortunately, it was not what I had hoped for.

The interview ( An Asian Guy) started with a discussion about my work experience at Google, which went smoothly. However, things took a turn during the coding challenge portion. I was tasked with implementing a topological sort ( to be in short ) for a graph—a problem I’m familiar with and confident in solving.

Here’s what happened:

I explained my approach, and the interviewer agreed that it was correct.
As I moved on to implement the solution, the interviewer seemed to struggle with understanding my code despite my efforts to clarify it step by step.
This led to a frustrating back-and-forth where the interviewer disagreed with my solution without providing clear reasoning. I attempted to explain my logic patiently, but the discussion felt more argumentative than constructive.
What was most disappointing was the way the interview concluded. After the session, the interviewer’s demeanor was unprofessional and dismissive, leaving me with a negative impression of the process.

I’ve reached out to the company, requesting a review of my performance by another panel or the opportunity for an additional round of interviews, as I feel this experience may have unfairly impacted my candidacy.

For anyone preparing for interviews, I’d advise staying calm and advocating for yourself if you face similar challenges. While candidates work hard to prepare, it’s equally important for interviewers to maintain professionalism and foster a respectful environment.

I hope Microsoft considers the importance of interviewer conduct in ensuring a positive candidate experience.

Thanks for Reading!

Edit1 : You may wonder  interviewer asks the same question repeatedly throughout countless interviews. How is it possible that he couldn’t understand my code? This wasn’t just about solving a random problem—it was actually about addressing a real issue they were facing in their work. The problem involved connecting nodes that were dependent on each other. Eventually, we concluded that we needed to use topological sorting. Once we identified this, the problem statement was completely reduced to finding a topological sort.

That’s it—that was the question. I’ve taught this question to many of my students and mentees, and I’ve even created a video on it for youtube community as well.

   - Given a string, replace the largest repeated substring at every point with an asterisk (*). The goal is to obtain a minimal-length string after compression.
   - Example 1: 
     - Input: `s = "abcabcd"`
     - Output: `"abc*d"` (Reason: Replace the second instance of "abc" with `*`.)

title: Amazon - SDE Internship - Brazil - Offer
page_content:
Hey guys, I want to share my experience going through the SDE Intership process for Amazon.


The whole process took about 3 months to finish, from the CV uploaded until the offer, which I thought was really slow, but much faster than some other cases I've seen out there...


I applied to the SDE Internship role at Amazon Brazil in S\xE3o Paulo. After applying, it took around one month to get the first response. It was a invite to take the OA and I had 15 days from recieving the email to finish it. (Although I've seen some people saying that it is better not to take too long to do it cause they may fill out your space with other candidate...)


When I got this email I knew that I had to start grinding Leetcode as much as possible. So I bought the premium plan and studied all the questions in the Amazon section. I think it was worth it... Not because paying for it gave me any advantage with different questions or information, but because having a better structured plan and questions to study helped me get confident and study properly...


After 10 days I decided to start the OA. I got 2 questions, which I think was 1 easy and 1 medium level. I really don't remember the topic on the first one, but it was really easy and I got all the test cases... The second one was a bit trickier and was basically greedy with multiples arrays, where you should merge and sort them to get the answer. I lost a lot of time going to the wrong track, but was able to figure out the solution in the end which I couldn't code up on time... I got only 10 out of 14 test cases...


This took once again 1 month to recieve another follow up... I thought I was out due to the second question, but no. I was invited to participate in the final round with two interviews, covering both behavioral and technical questions. Both of them occured in the same day, with two different interviewers.


The first one focused in my CV, so I really did not get any LP question in this one, he just scan through the things I've written in my CV asking how I accomplish this and did that... About 20 minutes in, we changed to the technical part in the shared code editor. I was asked a basic OOP modeling problem, such as "You have to solve this problem, how would you create classes to structure the solution? And what if this was different" kind of thing (I found it very interesting cause I haven't seen anyone getting this during Intership roles)... Then a basic problem where I needed to convert number of seconds to hours, minutes and seconds in HH:MM:SS format and with some weird edge cases and considerations.


The second asked me LP questions, I only remember being about Deliver Results... I also remember that it was a bit hard to understand his english accent. The technical part was a straight forward questions about trees. I had to build a tree with the employees of the a company, linking who is the boss of who, to make some traversing to find common bosses between 2 different employees and such. Had plenty of time to code and develop the solution and in the end he gave me a harder version of the question, which I did not had time to code, but I could go through the line of thought I had to solve it and went through the time and memory complexity for that.


In the end of both interviews I asked for a quick/small feedback, knowing that I wouldn't get any from that point on, It was my only chance to receive some kind of feedback. The first one said that I was good but could have asked more clarifying questions about the problem. The second said he liked my answers very much and he that from his point of view I would be a good co-worker :). (So don't be afraid to ask for a quick feedback). I was feeling very good about the results and my overall performance. But anything could happen...


Usually, they tell you that it takes around 5 working days for them to send you the final answer... So I waited for 5 days.... 1 week... 2 weeks... 1 month... and nothing... After 1 month I decided to send an email, asking for a followup, since I hadn't heard anything for a long time. After 2 hours that I sent the email, I received a message from the hiring manager, saying that mine got lost in the middle of a lot of candidates but I was approved, and would get the formal offer soon!


I accepted the offer and I am now waiting for the onboarding and documentation steps to begin! Thank you Leetcode and community, without you guys I wouldn't be able to get this achievement so early in my career... If anyone wants to know more about it, feel free to ask!

title: Expedia SDE-3 | Interview Experience | Oct 2024 | Rejected
page_content:
I applied in expedia Gurgaon via referral from a friend. Got a call from the recruiter after about a week. Since I was also a former employee of Expedia, they conducted a background check that took around 15 days before moving forward with the interview.


**Round 1 | Coding, Problem Solving** 
	* 	Started with questions about previous projects, the interviewer asked some followup questions on distributed systems and scaling
	* 	1 LC medium-hard question on DP (solved)
	* 	My laptop started hanging midway through the interview because of which about 10 minutes got wasted. The interviewer was very patient and cooperative, which I appreciated. He wanted to ask a second question but, due to the lost time, decided to skip it.
	* 	Overall, I was not quite satisfied with the round due to the above reason.

After about a week, I received a call that I had cleared the interview and next 3 rounds were scheduled.

**Round 2 | Coding, DS/Algo** 
	* 	2 LC medium questions on trees and stack (solved both)
	* 	The interviewer asked some follow up questions on my solutions. He also changed the questions a bit and asked me to modify the code which I was able to do optimally.

**Round 3 | Design HLD**
	* The Interviewer asked to design a book recommendation system which had the following properties
			* Users could create posts like book reviews, book recommendations etc which would have likes and comments.
			* Publishers could also create posts about book recommendations.
			* Users would get book recommendations from publishers as well as system.
			* Users could follow each other
	* initially, I started with designing a system for creating and storing posts, likes and comments. The discussion went around database designing for posts, likes and comments. Some discussion around aggregation of likes didn't go quite well. 
	* The interviewer was more interested on designing a system for system generated book recommendations. I went on with an approach of the system scraping posts of users and publishers to create a database which would contain the scoring of a book on various genres as well as user's interest score on various genres. I created a recommender service which would then create post for a particular user based on this interest and add it to the user's timeline. 
	* In my opinion, this round didn't go well as I was not able to give a satisfactory explaination for various aspects of the design.

**Round 4 | Technical Acumen, Overall Fitment**
	* The interviewer asked about my previous projects, my mentoring experience(which was not much), my most challenging project, a time when I displayed leadership.
	* We had a good interaction around these aspects and the interviewer also shared his experience and opinions which I found great.


Received the rejection call after a week.

Best of luck to anyone else applying!
